name: Tennis
tagline: A conversation in topspin — the oldest racket game still played for the biggest prizes.
overview: Tennis is played between two players (or two pairs) on a rectangular court divided by a net; the ball must be struck over the net and inside the lines so the opponent cannot return it before the second bounce. Matches are decided in sets, sets in games, games in points — a nesting structure that makes comebacks from any deficit mathematically possible and psychologically brutal.

It is the only major sport played on four surfaces — grass, clay, hard, and indoor carpet-lite — and each changes the game's grammar: grass skids low and rewards serving volleyers, clay slows the ball and builds armies of patience, hard courts split the difference. The four Grand Slams (Wimbledon 1877, US Open 1881, French Open 1891, Australian Open 1905) remain among the longest-running annual sporting events on Earth, and the Open Era since 1968 has made the tour a 12-month world circus.

Newcomers should learn scoring early (love, 15, 30, 40, deuce) because the rules make every game a small drama. The technical priority order is: consistent serve toss, reliable forehand rally ball, then the two-handed backhand — in that order. Everything else in tennis is built on landing those three under mild pressure.
facts: First codified
1874 — Major Walter Clopton Wingfield patents 'Sphairistikè'; the All England Club writes the modern rules for Wimbledon 1877
Governing bodies
International Tennis Federation (founded 1913 as the ILTF); ATP and WTA tours; six regional associations
Format
Singles or doubles; best of 3 or 5 sets; tiebreak at 6-6 (7 points, win by 2)
Court
23.77 m long × 8.23 m wide (singles; 10.97 m for doubles); net 0.914 m at center
Ball
Yellow-fluorescent, 6.54-6.86 cm diameter, 56.0-59.4 g; pressurized cans for match play
Olympic status
Played 1896-1924, restored as full medal sport since 1988 (Seoul)
Scoring quirk
Love-15-30-40-deuce; the 40-40 'deuce' requires a two-point margin — a rule inherited from French court games
history: 12th-16th c.
Jeu de paume — real tennis — is played by European nobility with the palm, then a racket; indoor courts survive at Wimbledon's name and Hampton Court.
Wingfield's boxed 'lawn tennis' kit sells across the Empire; croquet lawns are converted within a decade.
The four championships that become the Grand Slams are founded; Wimbledon's first champion, Spencer Gore, wins before a crowd of 200.
The ILTF forms; Suzanne Lenglen and Bill Tilden become the first global celebrities of the sport.
The Open Era begins — professionals are readmitted to the Slams, and the modern tour economy starts.
The ATP (players) and WTA (led by Billie Jean King, under the Virginia Slims circuit) unionize the professional game; the 1973 'Battle of the Sexes' King-Riggs match draws 90 million viewers.
1970s-today
The tiebreak, electronic line calling, and Hawk-Eye review (2006) modernize officiating; racket frames go wood → graphite (1980s) → modern carbon composites that make 200 km/h forehands routine.
formats: Singles
Two players; the purest form — one opponent, no partner to share glory or blame with.
Doubles & mixed
Four players; alleys widen the court, teamwork replaces rally patience, and reflex volleys decide points in under three shots.
Team competitions
Davis Cup (1900, men) and Billie Jean King Cup (1963, women) — nation versus nation across a season, finals weeks now hosted at single sites.
Fast4 & Tie-Break Tens
Shortened codes (first to 4 games, 10-point match tiebreaks) built for televised one-night events and league nights.
skills: Serve
The only stroke you fully control; variants are flat (speed), slice (curve away), and kick (twist up and into the returner's backhand).
Fifty serves per session in blocks of ten, two target boxes each for wide and T; log first-serve percentage, aim 60%+ landing.
Forehand drive
The dominant rally weapon: semi-western grip, unit turn, kinetic chain from legs through hip rotation to a high finish.
Cross-court consistency drill: 20 balls in a row inside the singles sideline before pace increases; then down-the-line on call.
Two-handed backhand
Compact, reliable, and blind to nerves — two hands stabilize the face through contact.
Coach feeds medium pace to the backhand; player hits 15 cross-court, 15 line; add approach shot on the 16th ball.
Return of serve
The most under-practiced match-winner: short split-step, compact take-back, depth over power.
Return practice against a server hitting at 70%: target the server's feet, deep middle, and alley — ten each.
Volley & overhead
Net play: punch volley with fixed wrists; overhead smash with a sideways stance and a thrower's motion.
Progressive volley drill: hand-feed, then racket-feed, then live; overheads from lobs, ten from each half of the court.
Footwork & split step
The split step lands as the opponent strikes; recovery steps return you to the correct court position after every shot.
Shadow tennis: hit-and-recover patterns (wide forehand → center, deep backhand → center) for 90 seconds on, 30 off, six rounds.
rules: Points run love-15-30-40, then game; at deuce (40-40), a player needs two straight points (advantage, then game).
Sets go to 6 games with a two-game margin; at 6-6 a 7-point tiebreak (win by 2) decides the set in most events.
The server gets two attempts; a foot crossing the baseline before contact is a fault. Alternates each point from deuce and ad courts.
A ball is in if any part of its mark touches any part of the line; first bounce only on your side in singles play.
Lets (serves clipping the net and landing in) are replayed; hindrance rules silence spectators between serves.
Coaching is permitted only at set breaks and changeovers on the main tours (a 2022-onward ATP/WTA liberalization).
Balls are changed every 7 (then 9) games; new balls fly faster off the racket and kick higher off the clay.
equipment: Racket
260-320 g strung for adults; head sizes 95-105 in². Beginner rackets ($50-100) favor light and forgiving; advanced frames ($180-250) demand better timing and reward it.
Strings & stringing

Polyester for control and spin (replace every 20-30 playing hours), multifilament for comfort; tension 21-27 kg — lower for power, higher for control. Stringing is the cheapest performance upgrade in the sport.
Shoes
Court-specific soles: herringbone for clay, modified tread for hard, pimples for grass. Running shoes roll ankles on tennis's lateral loading — do not.
Balls
Pressurized cans for matches ($4-6); pressureless for practice baskets. ITF-approved felt plays differently on clay (heavier duty) versus hard courts.
Grips & overgrips
Replace overgrip when slick (every 2-4 sessions, $2 each); correct grip size prevents elbow trouble.
Kit
Breathable polos/dresses, wristbands, a cap; grass-court events still enforce near-white dress at Wimbledon.
training: Build the tennis engine: repeated 5-10 second anaerobic efforts inside long matches — interval running (30 s hard / 30 s easy for 20-30 minutes) beats jogging.
Rotational strength: medicine-ball throws (forehand and backhand patterns, 3×8 each side) train the hips and trunk that actually produce serve speed.
Protect the shoulder and elbow: band work for rotator cuffs daily, and technical fixes before brace shopping — most tennis elbow is a late contact point, not weak tissue.
Serve and return volume: the two shots decide most matches at every level below professional — basket serves and return practice are non-negotiable twice a week.
Play practice sets weekly; patterns under score pressure (30-40, ad-out) teach decisions that drills cannot.
pathway: Junior tennis (U10-U18)
Red/orange/green low-compression balls by age; national ratings and junior tours (ITF World Tennis Tour Juniors) from 13+.
College tennis
NCAA route in the US — 4-year eligibility, world-class coaching, and degrees; a common springboard to the pro tour.
Transition tour
ITF Men's/Women's World Tennis Tour: $15k-$25k events where players grind for ATP/WTA ranking points.
ATP/WTA tour
Challengers → 250s/500s → Masters 1000/WTA 1000 → Grand Slams; the top ~100 make a living, the top 20 a fortune.
Senior & wheelchair tennis
Age-group worlds from 35+ and a full wheelchair tour with its own Slams — tennis genuinely runs cradle to grave.
events: Grand Slams
Australian Open (hard, January), French Open (clay, May-June), Wimbledon (grass, June-July), US Open (hard, August-September) — best of five sets for men at Slams.
ATP Finals & WTA Finals
Season championships for the year's top 8 — round-robin into a final, the tightest field in tennis.
Davis Cup & Billie Jean King Cup
National teams, 1900 and 1963 vintage; the World Cup of tennis, restructured into finals weeks since 2019.
Olympic tennis
Every four years since 1988; a gold medal is the rarest major, and the Golden Slam (all four Slams + gold in one year, Steffi Graf 1988) the rarest feat in the sport.
Masters 1000 / WTA 1000
Nine combined premium events (Indian Wells, Miami, Madrid, Rome, and more) that shape the year's rankings battle.
legends: Rod Laver
Australia — the only man to win the calendar Grand Slam twice (1962, 1969); the Open Era's measuring stick.
Serena Williams
USA — 23 major singles titles in the Open Era, power tennis' founding document, and four straight Slams across 2002-03.
Roger Federer · Rafael Nadal · Novak Djokovic
The Big Three: 66 combined majors; Federer's artistry, Nadal's clay kingdom (14 French Opens), Djokovic's 24-Slam record.
Margaret Court & Martina Navratilova
24 majors and 18 respectively; Navratilova's 167 singles titles and fitness revolution moved the whole sport professional.
Billie Jean King
USA — 12 majors, founder of the WTA, and the 1973 Battle of the Sexes; the sport's conscience and its progressive engine.
getting_started: Take three group lessons before buying anything serious; a coach's eye on your serve motion is worth any racket.
Start with one all-round racket (270-290 g), court shoes for your surface, and a hopper of pressureless balls — about $150 all in.
Learn to score in your first fortnight: play short sets to 4 games with friends so match tension arrives early.
Find your local ladder or club night within a month; tennis is a language best learned in conversation.
Practice the serve alone twice a week — it is the only stroke that needs no partner and wins the most free points.
Watch one ATP or WTA match a week with a single question: where does the server's first serve land, and where does the return go?
glossary: Ace
A serve the returner never touches — a point won with one swing.
Break point
A point which, if won by the returner, wins the game against the serve; 'three break points down' is tennis' quiet panic.
Deuce
40-40; from here you need two consecutive points — advantage, then game.
Golden Slam
All four majors plus Olympic gold in a single year (Steffi Graf, 1988).
Kick serve
A serve hit with heavy topspin-slice that jumps high and sideways — the second-serve workhorse.
Lob & drop shot
The sport's vertical pair: one floats over a net player, the other dies just over the net.
Love
Zero — from l'œuf, the egg, whose shape is a nought.
Rally & let
The exchange of shots; a serve clipping the net and landing fair is replayed as a 'let'.
Slice
Underspin that floats low and skids; defensive by default, deadly as an approach on grass.
Tiebreak
First to 7 points by 2 at 6-6, points counted plain and brutal — tennis compressed into five minutes.

name: Badminton
tagline: The fastest racket sport on Earth — a shuttle that leaves at 400 km/h and dies by the net.
overview: Badminton is played with feathered shuttles and light rackets across a 1.55 m net, as singles or doubles. The shuttle's drag makes it the great paradox of sport: record smashes exceed 400 km/h in lab tests, yet the same projectile can be coaxed into a drop shot that lands dead — so the game alternates between ballistic and surgical within a single rally.

It has been an Olympic sport since 1992 and is a national institution across Asia — Indonesia, Malaysia, China, India, Japan — where its stars are household names and Sudirman Cup and Thomas/Uber Cup weeks stop the country. Denmark carries the European flag with world-champion pedigree. It is also the world's most played racket sport by participation, precisely because a garden version needs almost nothing.

Newcomers should respect two things: the grip is a handshake, not a hammer (tight grips kill the snap that generates power), and footwork, not arm strength, gets you to the shuttle early. Hit from behind the shuttle whenever possible; the whole sport is arranged around buying yourself that fraction of a second.
facts: Modern codification
1873 at Badminton House, Gloucestershire; Bath Badminton Club writes first rules 1877; Badminton England (then ABA) 1893
Governing body
Badminton World Federation (1934 as IBF, renamed 2006); 200+ member associations
Court
13.40 m × 5.18 m singles, 6.10 m doubles; net 1.55 m at posts, 1.524 m center
Scoring
Rally-point to 21, best of 3 games; at 20-20 win by 2, cap at 30
Shuttle
16 feathers in a cork base, 4.74-5.50 g; match shuttles are feather (goose/duck), practice are nylon
Serve rule
Underarm, shuttle struck below 1.15 m (fixed-height rule since 2018), racket head pointing downward
Olympic status
Medal sport since Barcelona 1992; mixed doubles added Atlanta 1996
history: Mid-1800s
British officers in India play 'Poona' with battledores and shuttlecocks; they bring it home.
The Duke of Beaufort's Badminton House names the game; the Bath club and then the national association codify it.
The All England Open begins — badminton's Wimbledon, still played every March at Birmingham.
The IBF forms with nine nations; the Thomas Cup (men's teams, 1948-49) becomes badminton's first world team trophy.
Barcelona Olympics: badminton becomes a medal sport; Susi Susanti's gold triggers Indonesia's national celebration.
Rally-point scoring to 21 replaces the old service-over system; the IBF becomes the BWF — the modern game's rules settle.
formats: Singles
One on one in the narrowed court; a chess of clears, drops, and smashes built on reaching the four corners.
Doubles & mixed
Four players in the full court; flat drives, service battles, rotation on attack-and-defense — badminton's fastest theater.
Team cups
Thomas Cup (men), Uber Cup (women), Sudirman Cup (mixed) — national teams in ties of best-of-five.
AirBadminton
The BWF's outdoor code with a heavier AirShuttle, launched 2019 to take the game to parks and beaches.
skills: Grip & racket work
Forehand 'handshake' grip with relaxed fingers; the power comes from a forearm rotation (supination), never a stiff wrist.
Shadow swings checking grip looseness; 50 flat-wall taps and 50 finger-power lifts daily.
Clear
The high deep shot to the back tramline — the rally reset and the beginner's first weapon.
Multishuttle feeds to backcourt: 30 shuttles, target the last meter before the baseline; 3 sets.
Drop shot
The clear's evil twin: same preparation, feathered touch, dies just past the tape.
Half-court game with clears only allowed to set up drops; score 10 landings inside the front service line.
Smash
Overhead power stroke; contact in front and above, body arching through the hit.
Jump-smash technique with a coach's basket: 3×15 shuttles alternating straight and cross smashes at 70% power first.
Net play
Tumbling net shots, lifts, and kills within arm's reach of the tape.
Two-player net battle: soft shots only inside the front service line, first to 21 points; daily 5 minutes.
Footwork
Chassé, scissor kick, and the lunge that covers a court in 3-4 steps; recovery to base after every shot.
Corner-fetch drills: shadow to four corners on call, 45 seconds on/15 off, six rounds; add split-step timing.
rules: Rally scoring to 21; you must win by two (first to 30 at 29-29). Best of three games.
Serve is underarm from below 1.15 m, into the diagonally opposite service box; in doubles, service courts alternate with scoring.
A rally ends when the shuttle lands (point to the striker's side regardless of who served — rally point), or a fault: net, out, double-hit, or touching the net with body or racket.
In doubles after the serve, the full court is in play and partners may occupy any half — including the rotation switches on attack.
Shuttle landing on the line is in; let cords replayed only for service faults off the tape.
Change ends at 11 in each game and after each game; one 60-second interval at 11 and 2 minutes between games.
Coaching is allowed only in the intervals — a rule that makes mid-rally problem-solving the player's alone.
equipment: Racket
70-95 g today (carbon graphite); balance points shift head-light for doubles speed or head-heavy for singles power. $40 entry, $150-280 for top models.
Strings
High tension 24-28 lbs for control at advanced level, 18-22 for beginners' power and comfort; restring as often per month as you play per week.
Shuttles
Feather match shuttles (grade by speed 76-78) $25-35/dozen, last a game or two; nylon shuttles $2-3 each last months — the honest beginner choice.
Shoes
Non-marking gum-soled indoor court shoes with lateral support; badminton lunges wreck running shoes and ankles in weeks.
Grip & towel
Overgrips replaced weekly ($2), and a sweat towel — feather shuttles and humid courts make dry hands a real performance variable.
training: Train the energy system the match demands: elite rallies average under 10 seconds with 20-30 second rest — court sprints and shadow footwork intervals beat long slow runs.
Lunge strength is survival: Bulgarian split squats and lateral lunges 2× weekly; add Nordic-pattern work for the hamstrings that decelerate every retrieval.
Wrist and forearm endurance: rice-bucket or racket-speed exercises for the finger SNAP that powers clears — 10 minutes after play, not before.
Multishuttle feeding 2-3 times weekly is badminton's batting practice: it compresses a match's shot volume into fifteen minutes.
Play singles to build footwork and doubles to build reflexes; each fixes the other's weaknesses.
pathway: Junior & school badminton
Age-group state and national championships; badminton academies in Asia recruit from 8-10 years old.
National junior squads
Under-17 and under-19 international circuits (BWF World Junior Championships since 1992).
Senior international
BWF World Tour: International Challenge up to Super 1000 (All England, Indonesia, China Opens) — ranking points decide entries.
Continental teams & Olympics
Thomas/Uber/Sudirman Cups for country, then the Olympic draw of 38 per event — badminton's true summit.
Masters & para badminton
World Masters from 35+; para-badminton debuted at Tokyo 2020 with six sport classes.
events: Olympic Games
Every four years since 1992 — five golds: men's and women's singles and doubles, mixed doubles.
BWF World Championships
Annual (non-Olympic years historically, now annual) individual world titles since 1977.
All England Open
1899 vintage, March, Birmingham — badminton's Wimbledon and the title every player's resume wants.
Thomas & Uber Cups
Men's and women's world team championships, even years, since 1948-49 — national pride in a box.
Sudirman Cup
Mixed team worlds, odd years — men and women on one card, the format's best drama.
legends: Lin Dan
China — 'Super Dan': two Olympic golds (2008, 2012), five world titles, and the only man to defend Olympic singles gold.
Lee Chong Wei
Malaysia — three Olympic silvers and 69 weeks of world #1 in the era's greatest rivalry; a national hero at home.
Carolina Marín
Spain — Olympic champion 2016 and three world titles; broke Asia's grip on the women's game single-handedly.
Rudy Hartono
Indonesia — eight consecutive All England titles (1968-74 streak within a record total); the sport's first global icon.
Susi Susanti
Indonesia — the 1992 Olympic singles gold that founded a badminton-mad nation's modern era.
getting_started: Buy nylon shuttles, a 4U (80-84 g) even-balance racket, and proper indoor shoes — roughly $80-120 to be fully equipped.
Learn the 1.15 m serve rule and practice it alone against a wall mark; service faults lose more beginner games than smashes ever win.
Find a club night: badminton clubs are everywhere and famously welcoming to newcomers at B-level nights.
Do ten minutes of shadow footwork at home to each corner; footwork, not power, is what separates levels early.
Play both singles and doubles in your first two months — they teach different games and reveal which you love.
Watch one All England match per year at minimum; the footwork is visible and copyable.
glossary: Clear
A high, deep shot to the opponent's backcourt — the rally's reset button.
Drop shot
A soft shot from the rearcourt that dies just over the net; hit with the same preparation as a clear.
Drives
Flat, fast exchanges at net height, doubles' machine-gun rallies.
Service court & 1.15 rule
Serves travel diagonally into the service box, struck below fixed height 1.15 m.
Smash
The overhead kill; lab-recorded contact speeds exceed 400 km/h.
Hairpin net shot
A shuttle tapped from net height back over the tape, dropping like thread.
Let & fault
A service clipping the tape and landing in is replayed; net touches, double hits, and lifting the shuttle on serve are faults.
Rally point
Every rally scores for its winner, serve or receive — since 2006.
Split step
The little hop timed to the opponent's contact that makes fast players fast.
Tramlines
The side alleys: out for singles, in for doubles.

name: Table Tennis
tagline: Chess at 110 km/h — the world's most subtle two meters of table.
overview: Table tennis is played on a 2.74 × 1.525 m table across a 15.25 cm net, with small rackets and a 40 mm celluloid-free plastic ball. Its currency is spin: the best players generate more rotation than any other ball sport, and the game is really a conversation between topspin, backspin, and sidespin conducted at speeds that leave no time for thought.

An Olympic sport since 1988 and the pride of China — which has won 32 of 37 available Olympic golds since — it is also the world's great garage sport: a table in a basement has started uncounted national careers, and the ITTF counts 226 member associations. The sport's nickname, 'ping pong', is trademarked history; the game itself belongs to everyone.

Newcomers should know that spin beats speed at every level below expert. Learn to read opponent racket angle at contact, serve with intent from week one, and master the push and the loop before dreaming of kills — the ball that looks unreturnable is usually the one that comes back past you.
facts: Origins
1890s England as an after-dinner parlour game ('gossima', 'whiff-whaff'); celluloid balls from 1900
Governing body
International Table Tennis Federation, founded 1926, Vienna; 226 members
Table
2.74 m × 1.525 m, 76 cm high; net 15.25 cm; white lines 2 cm, center line for doubles
Ball
40 mm (since 2000), 2.7 g, plastic since 2014-15; orange or white
Scoring
Games to 11, win by 2; serve alternates every 2 points; matches best of 5 or 7
Olympic status
Medal sport since Seoul 1988; team events added 2008, mixed doubles Tokyo 2020
Speed & spin
Smashes pass 100-110 km/h; elite topspin exceeds 100 rotations per second
history: Parlour game patents and the first celluloid balls; the Ping-Pong Association forms in London (1902) and folds within years.
The ITTF is founded and Berlin hosts the first World Championships — still the sport's oldest continuous international event.
Japan's sponge rackets and the European-Japanese rivalry globalize technique; China wins its first world title in 1959 (Rong Guotuan).
'Ping-pong diplomacy': the US team's China tour helps thaw relations — table tennis literally enters geopolitics.
Olympic debut in Seoul; the 38 mm ball grows to 40 mm in 2000 to slow rallies for television.
2014-today
Celluloid gives way to plastic balls; rally lengths rise, and China's production line meets its first genuine resistance from Japan, Germany, and Sweden.
formats: Singles
Best of 5 or 7 games to 11; the classic duel of serve, receive, and third-ball attack.
Doubles
Alternate strokes per pair, serves diagonally into the right half-court; choreography in half-square spaces.
Team matches
Olympic format: best-of-five ties of singles (and one doubles since 2020) — the format that fills arenas in Asia.
Para table tennis
Eleven classes by impairment (standing and sitting), full Paralympic program since Rome 1960's first Games.
skills: Shakehand & penhold grips
Western shakehand dominates today; penhold (Chinese/Japanese) enables the fiercest forehand but a cramped backhand.
Ten minutes of grip checks and basic ball-bounce control (100 bounces forehand, 100 backhand) daily for beginners.
Serve & spin
The sport's ace in waiting: heavy backspin, no-spin 'ghost' serves, and sidespin curves struck behind the table's end line.
Two buckets a week: 50 serves each of backspin and sidespin to marked target halves; log how many come back short.
Push & touch play
The backspin answer to spin: short pushes over the table that keep the ball low and deny attack.
Push-to-push game inside the service zone only; first error loses — 10 games, count your unforced errors.
Loop (topspin drive)
The fundamental attack: brush the ball's back with an upward-forward arc; against backspin lift more, against block drive forward.
Multiball with a coach or robot: 3×30 forehand loops against backspin, then against blocks; alternate placement corners.
Backhand technique
Modern reverse backhands (and the penhold reverse) made two-winged attackers the standard.
Backhand-to-backhand count drills: 50 in a row at 70% pace before pace increases.
Footwork
Side-shuffle and in-out movement to keep the striking zone at the hip; the free arm balances the whole machine.
Falkenberg drill (backhand, forehand from the backhand corner, forehand from the wide forehand), 5 minutes continuous, 3 sets.
rules: Games to 11 points, win by 2; serve changes every 2 points, and at 10-10 every point.
The serve must start with the ball resting on an open flat palm, be tossed at least 16 cm vertically, and be struck behind the end line — hidden serves are illegal.
The ball must bounce once on each side; in doubles it must travel server's right half → receiver's right half, and partners alternate hits.
A point ends on: double bounce on one side, into the net or off the table, a volley struck before the ball bounces (obstruction), or moving the table.
Let serves (net clip, good bounce) are replayed; the edge ball off the table's vertical side is a point to the striker.
Racket surfaces must be red on one side, black on the other, and meet ITTF authorization lists; glues are regulated (speed-glue bans since 2008).
One timeout per player or pair per match; towel breaks at 6-point intervals.
equipment: Racket (blade + rubbers)
Wood blades (85% wood minimum) with rubber and sponge: fast carbon blades for attackers ($80-250), all-round wood for learners ($30-60); rubbers replaced when slick ($30-70 a sheet).
Balls
40+ mm plastic, three-star for match play ($1-2 each); one-star or training boxes for volume ($0.50 each in 100-packs).
Table
ITTF-standard 25 mm tops for clubs ($1,500+); 16-19 mm home tables ($400-800) play honestly for garage careers.
Shoes
Low, gum-soled indoor shoes for feel and lateral grip; running shoes are too cushioned for the sport's micro-steps.
Net & barrier kit
A clip-on net for home tables, and ideally barriers or a catch-net — one thousand fewer balls lost per year.
training: Multiball is the sport's laboratory: 200-400 balls a session against a coach or robot beats four hours of casual rallying.
Serve practice is completely solo and endlessly deep: three sessions a week, 100 serves each, with a notebook on what returns each serve earns.
Footwork fitness: side-to-side table-width sprints and in-out shadow steps, 20 seconds on/10 off, eight rounds — the game's actual energy demand.
Play up whenever possible: one weekly session against better players accelerates reading of spin faster than any drill.
Rotate practice partners' styles — a chopper, a pips-out blocker, and a looper each teach different reading problems.
pathway: School & club play
After-school programs and local leagues; national cadet (U15) and junior (U19) circuits from age 11.
National squads
Full-time training centers — the Chinese provincial system and its international imitations (Germany, Japan, Korea).
ITTF World Tour / WTT
World Table Tennis (2021-) events: feeder to contender to smash-level tournaments feeding the world ranking.
Worlds & Olympics
World Championships (individual odd years, team even) and the Olympic five-gold program.
Veterans & para
World Veterans Championships (40-80+) dwarf most sports' masters draws; para classes compete at the Paralympics.
events: Olympic Games
Since 1988: men's and women's singles and teams, plus mixed doubles since Tokyo 2020.
World Table Tennis Championships
Since 1926; the individual titles (odd years) and team titles (even years) are the sport's oldest crowns.
WTT Cup Finals & Grand Smashes
The professional circuit's season finals and the four super-events (Singapore, China, Saudi, Europe) of the modern calendar.
ITTF World Cup
Annual invitational (from 1980); the sport's sharpest short-format prize.
Continental championships
European Championships, Asian Championships — Europe vs Asia's annual measuring sticks.
legends: Deng Yaping
China — four Olympic golds and 18 world titles at 1.55 m tall; the most decorated woman of the sport's first century.
Jan-Ove Waldner
Sweden — 'the Evergreen': 1992 Olympic champion, the European genius who read spin like sheet music, competitive into his 40s.
Ma Long
China — the only double career Grand Slam winner (two of each: Olympics, Worlds, World Cup); the modern game's completed argument.
Zhang Yining
China — back-to-back Olympic singles golds (2004, 2008) and a win rate that made her era feel settled.
Viktor Barna
Hungary — five world singles titles (1930-35) with a hard bat; the sport's first great dynasty player.
getting_started: Buy an all-round premade racket ($40-60), a box of one-star balls, and find a table — club nights beat home tables for learning.
Learn the legal serve in week one: flat palm, 16 cm toss, behind the end line. Bad habits here take years to unlearn.
Practice push rallies to 50 in a row before attacking; low and slow wins beginner matches.
Do 10 minutes of daily bounce control on the racket at home — both faces, forehand and backhand.
Join a league within two months: table tennis leagues grade finely, so you will find your exact level fast.
Watch one Ma Long or Waldner match end to end; note how points are built on the third ball, not the first.
glossary: Loop
The topspin attack — brushing the ball into an arc that kicks forward off the bounce.
Push
A backspin reply over the table that keeps the ball low and unattackable.
Chop
Heavy backspin defense from mid-distance; choppers are the sport's contrarians.
Third-ball attack
The serve, the receive, and the planned kill that follows — where points are actually designed.
Penhold
The Asian grip with the racket held like a pen; fearsome forehands, distinctive footwork.
Pips (short/long)
Pimpled rubbers that deaden or reverse spin; the defender's and disruptor's toolkit.
Let & edge ball
Net-clipping serves replayed; balls off the table's vertical edge count for the striker — the sport's luckiest centimeters.
Multiball
Feeding drills where a coach delivers balls in continuous sequence — table tennis' batting practice.
Block & counterloop
The passive wall and the aggressive answer to topspin; the modern rally's grammar.
Free hand on the table
Touching the table with the non-racket hand loses the point — a rule beginners meet early.

name: Squash
tagline: A gladiatorial phone box — 130 heartbeats a minute against three walls and one opponent.
overview: Squash is played inside a four-walled court by two players who share the same space, taking turns to strike a small rubber ball above the tin and below the out line so the opponent cannot make a legal return. Because both players occupy one court, the game is part duel, part negotiation — shot selection must respect the opponent's position, and the rules (lets and strokes) police the collision.

Invented at Harrow School in the 1830s when pupils found a punctured rackets ball 'squashed' against walls offered a better game, it became the fitness connoisseur's racket sport: rally-intensity data has repeatedly crowned professional squash among the most aerobically brutal of all sports. Pakistan built a dynasty on it, Egypt owns it now, and in 2023 the IOC finally voted it onto the LA 2028 Olympic program.

Newcomers should know the ball barely bounces until warm (that thud against the tin is universal), the T — the court's crossroads — is home base to fight for, and hitting straight beats hitting clever. Learn the straight drive down the wall to the back corners and you have the sport's single most valuable shot.
facts: Origins
1830s Harrow School; the 'squash' name from the soft punctured rackets ball; first purpose courts at Harrow 1864
Governing body
World Squash Federation (1967 as ISRF); professional tours PSA (1975-merged) and PSA Women's (2015 merged under PSA)
Court
9.75 m × 6.4 m; front line 'tin' 48 cm high; out lines 4.57 m front / 2.13 m back at 1.78 m height; minimum 4 m ceiling play
Ball
Single dot to double yellow dot by speed (double yellow = pro/advanced, slowest, high bounce only when warm); 40 mm, 24 g rubber
Scoring
Point-a-rally to 11, best of 5 games (PAR 11, universal since 2009)
Olympic status
Voted into the Los Angeles 2028 program in October 2023 after five failed bids — the sport's century-late debut
history: Harrow boys discover a punctured rackets ball squashes into walls and plays truer in cramped school yards; the game is born an accident.
Harrow builds the first four purpose courts; the Tennis & Rackets Association publishes the first squash rules in 1907.
Britain's Empire exports the game; the (British) Squash Rackets Association forms 1928; Egypt's colonial clubs seed a future superpower.
Pakistan's Jonahangir-Jansher era approaches: hardball squash thrives in North America alongside the international softball code.
Jahangir Khan's 555-match unbeaten run (1981-86) — among the longest streaks in any professional sport.
Dunlop's double-yellow standardizes the ball; glass courts take finals to Grand Central and Cairo opera houses; LA 2028 finally calls squash Olympic.
formats: Singles (softball)
The international 21 ft game, PAR 11 to 11 best of five — the world standard and the Olympic format.
Hardball singles
The North American 18.5 ft court with a faster ball and pars of 15; a heritage code still played in US clubs.
Doubles
A wider 25 ft court, bouncier ball, four players — common in North America and growing on the PSA Doubles circuit.
Team & league squash
Club ladders, county and national leagues, and the biennial World Team Championships; college squash in the US is an institution.
skills: Straight drive
The sport's spine: ball hit parallel to the side wall into the back corner, ideally with the second bounce dying.
Length ladders: solo drive to a target behind the service box, 3×30 forehand and backhand; two-wall errors counted as misses.
Boast
The three-wall angle that drives the ball into the front wall via the side wall — the rear-court escape and the deception tool.
Pairs routine: drive-drive-boast continuous for 10 minutes; boast must land in the front quarter to count.
Drop shot & lob
The vertical pair: a kill into the front corner nick or a lob over the opponent's head into the back corner.
Feed-and-finish: coach feeds medium drives, player alternates drop and lob, 20 reps each side; drops must bounce twice before the tin line.
Volley
Taking the ball before the bounce — steals time, controls the T, and wins matches at every level.
Volley-to-length pairs drill: everything taken in the air into the back corners, 15 minutes continuous.
Movement to the T
Recovery to the T after every shot; lunges in, push out, never watch your own ball twice.
Ghosting: hit-and-recover patterns to front corners and back corners, 45 s on / 15 s off × 6; aim for T arrivals inside one second.
Serve & return
The high hard serve into the back corner deep; the return played cross-court or straight with depth.
Serve target zones behind the service box: 20 serves each side; returns drilled to force one more weak ball.
rules: PAR 11 scoring: every rally scores; games to 11 by two; best of five.
A legal return must strike the front wall above the tin and below the out line, and — unless volleyed — may first bounce once on the floor.
After serving from inside the service box (one foot inside, no touching lines), play alternates until a ball bounces twice, goes out, or a fault.
Interference is governed, not ignored: a blocked path earns a let (replay) or a stroke (point) depending on whether the striker could have reached the ball and where the opponent stood.
Turning (spinning to play a ball passing behind) is allowed once; striking the opponent with ball or racket is the opponent's point or a let by situation.
Warm-up is 5 minutes (2½ each side); the ball must be warm before rallies mean anything — double-yellow balls bounce only near game temperature.
Conduct penalties (conduct stroke, game, match) police dangerous play and abuse; protection of the opponent outranks the rally.
equipment: Racket
500 g max, teardrop or bridged heads; 120-135 g frames. $60 beginner, $180-280 pro-spec; strings snapped monthly by hard hitters.
Balls
Dunlop double yellow (pro), single yellow, blue dot by level — $3-5 each; buy three, warm two.
Shoes
Indoor court shoes with gum soles and lateral cages — squash lunges and pivots punish running shoes; replace when the sole smooths ($90-140).
Eyewear
Polycarbonate protective glasses: mandatory in junior and doubles play, strongly advised always — the ball and racket share your air.
Grip & towel
Overgrips changed weekly; sweat management is real in a glass box at 30 °C.
training: Interval engine: rallies of 20-60 seconds with 20-second gaps — court sprints, ghosting, and bike repeats match the demand better than steady running.
Lunge-and-push strength: rear-foot-elevated split squats, lateral lunges, and calf work twice weekly — squash's leg patterns in the weight room.
Core rotation: cable woodchops and med-ball rotational throws (3×8 each side) put pace on the ball without racket-arm strain.
Solo hitting is squash's meditation: 20 minutes of length ladders on a free court upgrades technique faster than any gadget.
Condition games (drops only, volleys only, one-serve) force specific skills under fatigue — finish every session with games that matter.
pathway: Club & school squash
Club ladders and school teams; junior bronze-silver-gold tournament tiers in most national systems.
Junior international
World Junior Championships and British Junior Open — the latter long the sport's undisputed proving ground.
PSA Challenger Tour
The professional entry tier: points, draws, and learning to win in foreign courts.
PSA World Tour
Copper to platinum events; the World Tour Finals for the season's top eight.
Worlds, teams, Olympics
Individual World Championship (since 1976 men / 1979 women), World Teams, and from 2028 the Olympic draw.
events: PSA World Championships
The individual world title, since 1976 — the sport's oldest crown and biggest purse weeks.
British Open
1922 vintage — squash's Wimbledon, its honor roll the game's history book.
World Team Championships
Biennial national teams; Egypt's current dynasty against England, France, and the resurgent pack.
PSA World Tour Finals
Season-ending top-eight knockout, glass court, one city — the tour's showcase week.
Olympic Games — Los Angeles 2028
Squash's debut: singles draws, glass court, a century of waiting answered.
legends: Jahangir Khan
Pakistan — ten British Opens, six world titles, and 555 consecutive match wins (1981-86): the longest streak in professional sport.
Jansher Khan
Pakistan — eight world championships and 99 tour titles; the two Khans ruled two decades between them.
Heather McKay
Australia — 16 consecutive British Opens (1962-77) and two world titles, losing twice in nineteen years: the most dominant record in racket sport.
Nicol David
Malaysia — eight world titles and a record 108 consecutive months at world #1 (2006-2015).
Mohamed ElShorbagy & Ali Farag
Egypt — the modern dynasty's twin pillars: ElShorbagy's two world titles and Farag's long #1 reign carry Cairo's factory line.
getting_started: Book a club court with a friend who has played once; buy a racket, a single-dot ball, and court shoes ($120 to start).
Learn length before flair: 20 minutes of straight drives down the wall is a complete first session.
Warm the ball properly (two minutes of firm rallying) — a cold double-yellow is a different, demoralizing sport.
Learn the let-and-stroke basics early so games stay friendly; interference rules are etiquette written down.
Join the club ladder in month two — the ladder is squash's matchmaking genius and its social engine.
Watch one Egyptian pro match (ElShorbagy, Farag, or the Gohar/El Sherbini women's finals) — note how little they hit off the back wall.
glossary: T
The court's crossroads where service boxes meet; owning it owns the angles.
Tin
The metal strip at the base of the front wall — 48 cm of humiliation; below it is out.
Boast
Any shot using a side (or back) wall before the front wall; the three-wall boast is the classic.
Nick
The junction of wall and floor where a dying ball stops bouncing — the drop shot's destination.
Let & stroke
Replay or penalty point awarded under interference rules; the sport's traffic law.
Ghosting
Movement training without a ball: hit, recover to the T, repeat to exhaustion.
Length
Depth — drives that pin the opponent in the back corners; the sport's first commandment.
PAR 11
Point-a-rally scoring to 11: every rally scores, so every error costs.
Broken ball
A ball that cracks mid-match is replaced after the rally; old balls cost you accuracy, not just bounce.
Conduct stroke
The referee's escalation for dangerous or abusive play — a point penalty on the spot.

name: Racquetball
tagline: Squash's American cousin — every wall is in play, including the ceiling.
overview: Racquetball is played on an enclosed 40 × 20 ft court where every surface — front wall, side walls, back wall, and ceiling — is legally in play. There is no tin to clear and no out-of-bounds above the front wall's service line zone: the ball may travel anywhere, which turns rallies into three-dimensional pinball played with a strapping blue ball that moves fast and bounces true.

Invented in 1950 by Joe Sobek, a tennis and squash professional who wanted a fast, learnable indoor game, racquetball boomed through 1970s America as the fitness-racket sport — at its peak more Americans played it than squash. Today it thrives most in Mexico, Bolivia, and the US, with the LPRT women's tour among the most professionally run circuits in any niche sport.

Newcomers should celebrate two gifts: the ball's liveliness forgives mistimed shots, and the serve is the sport's decisive weapon — drive serves and Z-serves that pin receivers deep. Learn ceiling ball as the rally-reset (the defensive shot that buys time), and the pinch shot as the finisher, and the game's geometry teaches itself.
facts: Invented
1950, Greenwich CT — Joseph Sobek combines paddleball and squash rackets with a strung racket; initially 'paddle rackets'
Governing bodies
International Racquetball Federation (1979); USA Racquetball (1968 as AARA); LPRT (women's pro tour, 1990s-present)
Court
12.2 m × 6.1 m × 6.1 m high (40 × 20 × 20 ft); no tin; ceiling in play after the serve's required front-wall-first contact
Ball
Bouncy blue rubber (2.25 in), the recreational standard; faster purple/red for pros by condition
Scoring
Rally scoring to 15 (win by one, or by two in some codes) with 11-point tiebreak; serve must land in the back quarter beyond the short line
Brief Olympic near-miss
Demonstration sport at the 1988 US Olympic Festival era; IRF recognized by the IOC (ARISF member) but never on the program
history: Joe Sobek strings a paddleball paddle in Greenwich, Connecticut, invents the game to stay fit indoors, and markets the rules himself.
The Amateur Racquetball Association of America forms (1968) with Robert Kendler's push; the first national championships follow (1969).
An estimated 10+ million Americans play; courts are built into nearly every new gym; the pro tour is televised.
The IRF forms and the first World Championships are held (1981); Mexico and Canada build pipelines that will rival the US.
The women's tour (later LPRT) professionalizes; Mexico's Paola Longoria begins her record dynasty (2009-present era).
Kane Waselenchuk rewrites the men's record book across two decades; Bolivia and Mexico flood the top rankings — the sport's center of gravity shifts south.
formats: Singles
The core game: two players, rally scoring to 15, best of five in championship play.
Doubles
Four players share the court with alternating-hit rules — racquetball at its most chaotic and social.
Cutthroat
Three players, one court: server versus both receivers rotating; the classic lunchtime club solution to odd numbers.
International & outdoor
IRF Worlds, Pan Am Games program; 'outdoor' 1-wall and 3-wall variants thrive in US parks (WOR — World Outdoor Racquetball).
skills: Drive serve
The point-winning weapon: low, hard serves into the corners that jam or ace receivers.
Bucket of 40 serves into marked corner zones, alternating power and Z; count aces and weak returns per zone.
Z-serve
The corner-curving serve off the side wall that handcuffs receivers deep in the court.
20 Z-serves each side; the ball must front-wall-first, side-wall second, and cross the receiving line deep.
Ceiling ball
The rally reset: a high, soft shot off the ceiling that forces the opponent deep and buys recovery time.
Pairs drill: under pressure, everything resets to ceiling for 10 minutes; ceiling shots must land behind the dashed receiving line.
Pinch shot
The low kill into the front corner via the side wall — the rally ender when the ball sits up.
Feed-and-finish: medium feeds to the forehand, alternate pinch and pass, 20 reps; pinches must double-bounce before the back of the service box.
Splat
The high-speed side-wall kill struck from beside the receiver — brutal, flashy, situational.
Practice only after pinch mastery: 10 splats per session, aiming the side-wall contact half a meter from the front wall.
Backwall play
Turning defense into attack: reading the ball's rebound and taking it off the glass early.
Deep court feeds: player starts behind the dashed line, must return to center by the third shot; 15 minutes.
rules: Rally scoring (LPRT/IRF standard) to 15 points; games must be won by one (two in some club codes), best of three or five.
The serve must bounce once, be struck toward the front wall first, and — beyond contact — land past the short line and inside the back quarter of the court.
Two serve attempts (sideout after two faults); a serve long off the back wall untouched is out.
Once in play, the ball may touch any number of walls/ceiling after hitting the front wall; it must be struck before its second floor bounce.
Hinders: blocked swings or screens replay the rally (dead-ball hinder); avoidable hinders cost the point.
Safety: the striker must give the opponent a direct view and path; hitting an opponent with the ball ends the rally by situation — protective eyewear is mandatory in sanctioned play.
Roster note: doubles partners alternate serves per sideout rather than per point, a quirk versus tennis.
equipment: Racket
22 in max, teardrop and quadraform heads with big sweet spots; $50-80 beginner, $150-250 pro models; strings cut and restrung ($25).
Balls
USRA blue (standard speed) $3-4; purple for pro; red for outdoor altitudes; buy a 3-can and warm two per match.
Shoes
Gum-soled indoor court shoes — the sport's lunges and pivots demand lateral cages ($80-140).
Eyewear
Mandatory in sanctioned play and always wise: the ball shares the court's air at 150 km/h.
Gloves & grips
A tacky glove ($15-25) or fresh overgrip keeps control through long rallies; sweat is the real opponent.
training: Train intervals of 15-40 seconds with short rests — court sprints and ghost drills mirror rally demands precisely.
Rotational and posterior-chain strength twice weekly: med-ball rotational throws, deadlifts, and lateral lunge patterns.
Serve practice alone is free wins: 100 serves a week split between drive and Z, with target zones taped on the floor.
Ceiling-ball rallies to 50 without error teach patience and build the lunging engine the game feeds on.
Play cutthroat when numbers are odd — it triples decision-making reps per hour.
pathway: Club & league play
Club ladders, city leagues, and USAR-sanctioned amateur tiers (gold/silver).
Junior national track
Junior Worlds (IRF) and high-school championships; Mexico and Bolivia recruit young into academies.
Collegiate & open
US college club championships and open prize events bridge amateurs to touring pros.
Pro tours
IRT (men) and LPRT (women): full professional calendars with season-ending finals.
Masters & worlds
Age-group worlds from 35+ to 80+, and IRF World Championships biennially — lifelong lanes.
events: US Open Racquetball Championships
Since 1996, Minneapolis and beyond — the sport's flagship week, glass court, streamed worldwide.
IRT & LPRT pro tours
Season-long professional circuits with rankings; the LPRT's consistency is a model for niche sports.
IRF World Championships
Biennial national-team worlds since 1981 — the USA-Mexico-Bolivia axis at full strength.
Pan American Games
Racquetball on the Pan Am program since 1995 — the sport's biggest multi-sport stage before an Olympic bid.
World Outdoor Racquetball (WOR)
The 3-wall park circuit: California and Florida's sun-bleached, beach-culture variant.
legends: Kane Waselenchuk
Canada/USA — the most dominant player ever: multiple US Open titles, long #1 reigns across two decades, and near-flawless win rates at his peak.
Paola Longoria
Mexico — the women's GOAT: multiple world titles and a decade-plus atop the LPRT, virtually unbeaten at her peak.
Cliff Swain
USA — the 1990s superstar whose power game and showmanship carried the early pro tour.
Sudsy Monchik
USA — five US Open titles and the left-handed power game that modernized professional racquetball in the 1990s.
Rubén González & Rhonda Rajsich
Longevity and grit: González's 25-year pro career and Rajsich's multiple world titles bookend the sport's heart.
getting_started: Find a court (gyms, YMCAs, universities) and rent or borrow a racket first session; buy your own after three visits.
Start with a blue ball — its speed is the friendliest possible introduction to the walls.
Learn the serve rules precisely (short line, back quarter); serves decide beginner racquetball outright.
Play the ceiling ball whenever uncertain — it is the sport's reset button and safest habit.
Wear eye protection from day one; the ball does not negotiate.
Join a league in month two: racquetball's club culture is famously social, and leagues fix your level instantly.
glossary: Ceiling ball
The defensive lob off the ceiling that resets the rally and drives the opponent deep.
Pinch
A low kill into the front corner struck via the near side wall.
Splat
A violent side-wall kill taken close to the wall — the highlight-reel finisher.
Z-serve
A serve angled into the side wall to curve across the receiving zone.
Short line & back line
The serve's landing window: beyond the short line, inside the final quarter of the court.
Screen serve
A serve that rebounds so close to the server the receiver cannot see it — a fault.
Hinder
Interference that kills the rally and forces a replay; avoidable hinders cost points.
Cutthroat
The three-player rotation game: one server against two receivers.
Skip ball
A shot that hits the floor before the front wall — the rally-losing error.
Rollout
The perfect kill: the ball rolls, it does not bounce, and the rally is over.

name: Padel
tagline: Tennis rebuilt inside a glass box — the fastest-growing court sport on the planet.
overview: Padel is doubles only, played with solid stringless rackets on an enclosed court about a third the size of a tennis court, where the ball may bounce off the back and side glass and mesh walls after crossing the net. The walls make rallies long, angles creative, and the game unusually social: points are built with walls rather than ended with serves, which is why beginners rally meaningfully within their first hour.

Invented in 1969 by Enrique Corcuera in Acapulco, padel became Argentina's and Spain's addiction — Spain alone has more than 20,000 courts — and in the 2020s it has spread across Europe, the Middle East, and beyond as the fastest-growing racket sport in the world, with a professional circuit (Premier Padel) now consolidated under the FIP.

Newcomers from tennis must unlearn one instinct: never smash out of panic, because the walls return the ball to the opponent's favor. Learn the bandeja (the tray-height control volley), the víbora (the aggressive angled variant), and wall play — bajada and contrapared — and padel's whole grammar opens up.
facts: Invented
1969 — Enrique Corcuera builds the first walled court at his Acapulco home; Alfonso of Hohenlohe imports it to Marbella 1974
Governing body
International Padel Federation (FIP, 1991); professional circuit Premier Padel (2021), consolidated with World Padel Tour 2023-24
Court
20 m × 10 m enclosed: back glass walls 3 m (4 m corners in arenas) + mesh above; service lines at 6.95 m; net 0.88 m
Racket (pala)
Solid, perforated, stringless composite — max 45.5 cm long, 26 cm wide; no strings means touch replaces power
Scoring
Identical to tennis (15-30-40, games, sets, tiebreaks); serve underhand, bounced first, struck below waist
Format
Doubles only, at every level in the world — there is no professional singles padel
history: Enrique Corcuera walls in a court at Acapulco to stop balls rolling into neighboring property — the walls become the game.
Prince Alfonso of Hohenlohe builds courts at Marbella Club; Argentine millionaire Julio Menditegui imports the game to Buenos Aires.
Argentina industrializes the sport (courts, clubs, coaches); Spain follows; the first national federations form.
The FIP is founded in Madrid; the first world championships are played (1992-93 era).
World Padel Tour professionalizes the pro game; Argentina and Spain split the era's titles.
2021-today
Qatar-backed Premier Padel launches (with FIP), merges with World Padel Tour (2023-24): one calendar, bigger purses, Olympic-recognized status via FIP.
formats: Professional doubles
Best of 3 sets, tennis scoring, golden point at deuce (deciding point) on the pro tour.
Amateur club padel
Identical rules, endless levels: club rankings, Americanos (group rotation formats), and weekend leagues.
Mixed & veterans
Growing FIP veterans worlds and mixed events; the sport's sociability drives mixed play hard.
Pop padel / mini padel
Youth development formats with scaled courts, the pipeline in Spain and Argentina.
skills: Bandeja
The signature shot: a cut volley taken at tray height from the midcourt, slow and angled to hold the net position without smashing.
Basket feeds at shoulder height: 3×20 bandejas to the corner glass, alternating flat-slice and cut.
Víbora
The aggressive sibling: sidespin volley struck smaller and faster, aimed to stay low off the glass.
Feed-and-finish pairs drill: 20 víboras each side after a bandeja sets up the weak reply.
Wall play (bajada & contrapared)
Taking the ball off the back glass (bajada, after the bounce) or the side/back wall without a bounce (contrapared) — padel's survival kit.
Coach hits deep balls into the glass: player returns 30 bajadas to the opponent's backhand corner; then 20 side-wall contrapared recoveries.
Serve & return
Underhand, bounced serve with slice; the return is played defensively to the server's feet or deep lob — never a winner's swing.
Serve target practice to the T glass (40 balls); returns drilled to two targets: backhand corner deep, and lob over the net player.
Lob & chiquita
The vertical escape and the mini-drop: the lob buys the net; the chiquita (slow, low ball to the feet) unpicks net rushers.
Pairs: after every smash, one chiquita to the feet is mandatory before any power — 15 minutes.
Smash (remate) & rulo
The padel smash is pulled down with topspin to return off your own back glass (a winning 'rulo' or by-the-wall kill); positioning decides more than power.
Fed smashes from the ideal contact zone: 30 reps aiming the second bounce to kick off the back glass; log direct winners.
rules: Scoring is exactly tennis: 15-30-40-game, six games per set (by two), tiebreaks at 6-6; matches best of three.
The serve must bounce once, be struck below waist height with an underarm swing, and land in the diagonal service box; glass counts as a fault (must hit the ground first).
After serve, the ball may bounce on the floor and then any wall — or hit a wall directly if it first crossed the net and touched the opponent's ground.
Players may even run out the door (where courts have them) to return a ball around the outside of the side wall — the around-the-wall and 'door' plays are legal.
The ball is out only if it hits a wall or fence before crossing the net, or bounces on the floor twice before being struck.
Both partners may hit alternately (any order after serve); typical positioning is one up, one back in transition and both at net when attacking.
Pro tour uses the golden point at deuce (next point wins the game); amateur play often follows suit.
equipment: Pala (racket)
Round (control), teardrop (all-round), or diamond (power) shapes in composite; $60-150 honest beginner range, $200-350 pro stock — buy control first.
Balls
Padel-specific pressurized balls, slightly lower pressure than tennis; $6-9 per 3-can.
Shoes
Herringbone gum-soled court shoes with lateral support — the 'galleta' (pancake) sole is the classic; running shoes roll ankles.
Court & glass
The 20×10 m cage: 10-12 mm tempered glass backs, steel mesh sides — the arena IS the equipment.
Overgrips & wrist cord
The safety cord (mandatory in play) stops flying palas; fresh overgrips weekly.
training: Wall-ball literacy is the sport's real skill: 15 minutes of solo bajada and contrapared work per session upgrades rating fastest.
Padel's engine is repeat efforts of 10-30 seconds: court intervals and shadow movement to the three zones (net, transition, back).
Rotational core and shoulder health: band work daily, med-ball rotational throws 3×10 each side — the bandeja is a shoulder tax.
Play Americanos weekly: rotation formats multiply different partners, styles, and pressure situations per hour.
Lob accuracy is fitness: 50 lobs a session to land inside the last meter before the glass — the most underrated winning shot.
pathway: Club padel
Book-and-play culture; club rankings and internal leagues from week one.
Amateur federation events
National amateur circuits and FIP-promotion stops; rating categories (1st to 7th in Spain's system).
Junior academies
Argentina and Spain run full-time junior high-performance centers; the pro pipeline runs through them.
Premier Padel tour
The unified professional circuit: majors, majors of the tour (P1/P2), and the Final — 32-pair draws, world ranking points.
Worlds & Olympic track
FIP World Padel Championships (biennial national teams, since 1992) and recognized-sport status on the road to the Games.
events: Premier Padel Major tournaments
The circuit's four Majors (Paris-Roland Garros among the iconic venues) — padel's Slams.
Premier Padel Finals
Season-ending top-pairs knockout, the tour's showcase.
FIP World Padel Championships
Biennial national teams since 1992 — Argentina and Spain's historic duel, now with 16+ nations competitive.
National circuits
Spain's and Argentina's professional circuits feed the tour; Italy, Sweden, Mexico, and the US grow theirs fast.
European & regional cups
FIP Euro Cup and confederation events spread the game beyond its two superpowers.
legends: Fernando Belasteguín
Argentina — 'Bela': 16 years at world #1 (2002-2018 era), the sport's standard of excellence and longevity.
Juan Lebrón
Spain — the first Spanish #1, an athletic net monster who brought tennis-bred explosiveness to padel.
Ale Galán
Spain — multiple year-end #1 with Lebrón in the sport's dominant pairing era 2019-2023.
Ari Sánchez & Paula Josemaría
Spain — the women's #1 pairing whose trophy run defined the early 2020s.
Gemma Triay
Spain — long-time world #1 and multiple Premier Padel Major titles; the women's game's anchor star.
getting_started: Book a court with three friends — padel is unplayable solo; one of you needs only beginner enthusiasm.
Buy a round control pala ($60-100) — power shapes punish beginners' timing.
Learn wall play before smash hunger: practice returning your own throw off the back glass for ten minutes every session.
Serve underarm and return deep; the first hour's goal is rallies, not winners.
Join your club's Americano night in week two — the format meets you at your exact level.
Watch one Premier Padel final: copy where players stand after the lob, not how hard they hit.
glossary: Bandeja
The tray-height cut volley that keeps the net without smashing.
Víbora
The snake: a smaller, faster, sidespin volley that stays low off the glass.
Bajada
The descending counter taken after the ball rebounds off the back glass.
Contrapared
A return played off the side or back wall without letting it bounce.
Chiquita
A deliberately slow, low ball to the feet — the game's picklock.
Rulo
The smash hit so it rolls off the smasher's own back wall for a winner.
Golden point
The deciding point at deuce on the pro tour.
Americanos
The rotating group format that powers club padel nights.
Pala
The stringless racket; also the sport's gear vocabulary word.
Rebote
Rebound — padel's essential verb; everything rebound-adjacent is technique.

name: Pickleball
tagline: A kitchen, a whiffle ball, and the fastest-growing sport in America.
overview: Pickleball is played with solid paddles and a perforated polymer ball on a badminton-sized court (20 × 44 ft) with a tennis-style net lowered to 34 inches. Its genius is the two rules that shape everything: the serve is underhand and unspun, and the seven-foot non-volley zone — the kitchen — forbids volleying close to the net. Together they make rallies long, placement decisive, and the game playable at high level by eight-year-olds and eighty-year-olds in the same morning.

Invented in 1965 on a Bainbridge Island driveway by congressman Joel Pritchard and friends who lowered a badminton net for their bored families, pickleball spent fifty years as a quiet retiree pastime — then became the fastest-growing sport in the United States for years running, with thousands of dedicated courts and a professional explosion (PPA Tour, Major League Pickleball) that dragged tennis stars across.

Newcomers should internalize one pattern above all: the third-shot drop. Serve, return deep, then glide the third ball softly into the kitchen so your team can reach the net — because in pickleball, the team at the net usually wins the point. Master that and the dink game, and the sport's chessboard opens.
facts: Invented
1965 — Joel Pritchard, Barney McCallum, and Bill Bell improvise a game on a Bainbridge Island, WA badminton court
Governing bodies
USA Pickleball (1984 as USAPA); International Federation of Pickleball (2010); professional leagues PPA, MLP (merged ownership 2023-24 era)
Court
6.1 m × 13.41 m (20 × 44 ft); net 0.86 m at center (34 in); kitchen 2.13 m (7 ft) from net on both sides
Ball
Perforated polymer, 26-40 holes: outdoor (heavier, 40 holes) and indoor (lighter, 26 holes) variants
Scoring
Games to 11, win by 2; side-out scoring in traditional doubles (only the serving team scores); rally scoring spreading in recreational and some pro formats
Name
Officially after the 'pickle boat' (rowing's leftover crew) per the Pritchard family — the dog-cute Pickles story came second
history: The Pritchard-McCallum-Bell afternoon on Bainbridge Island: badminton net lowered, whiffle balls, improvised plywood paddles.
A permanent court is built in a neighbor's backyard; the first known pickleball tournament follows in 1976.
The USAPA publishes the first rulebook and holds the first national championships; the composite paddle era begins.
Sunbelt retirement communities adopt the game wholesale; court conversions begin quietly.
The US Open Pickleball Championships (Naples, 2016) launches; participation doubles and doubles again.
Pickleball is America's fastest-growing sport for years straight; pro leagues (PPA, MLP) sign TV deals, prize money balloons, and tennis majors' champions switch codes.
formats: Doubles (traditional)
The heart of the game: side-out scoring to 11, two partners, the classic serve-and-kitchen duel.
Singles
Aerobic and angular: one player covering 20 feet of width with deep returns and drives — a different, harder sport.
Mixed doubles
Huge recreational and growing pro category; MLP's mixed team format has become its own show.
MLP team format
Major League Pickleball: gendered doubles, mixed doubles, and dream-breaker tiebreakers (singles rotation) — team pickleball built for broadcast.
skills: Serve & return depth
The serve is underhand, unspun, deep; the return is hit deep and followed to the net — returns that stay back lose.
Ten serves per session to a taped target zone near the baseline; returns drilled cross-court deep, then followed to the kitchen line.
Third-shot drop
The signature skill: a soft shot from the baseline into the kitchen that lets the serving team advance to the net.
Drop drills from the baseline to a kitchen target: 3×20, counting balls that land unattackable; progress to live serve-return-drop.
Dinking
The soft volley exchange played from the kitchen line: paddles up, balls low over the net, patience until a ball sits up.
Kitchen-line dink battles: 10-minute sessions where the ball must stay soft; first to force an attackable ball wins the exchange.
Volley & counterspeed
Punch volleys at the line: compact, firm, aimed at the opponent's right hip or the middle seam.
Volleys fed from midcourt: 3×15 with footwork checks — feet must be behind the kitchen line at contact.
Drives & resets
The hard flat drive as a change-up, and the reset (softening a hard ball back into the kitchen) — the game's gear-shifting pair.
Live drills: partner drives at 70%, player resets softly into the kitchen, 20 reps; count resets landing unattackable.
Lob & overhead
The lob over net-huggers and the putaway overhead — used less than in tennis, decisive when earned.
Fed lobs from the kitchen line: 15 returns, then 10 overheads placed to the open court.
rules: Games to 11, win by 2 (traditional); in doubles, only the serving team scores and both partners serve before side-out.
The serve is underarm or drop-serve, contacted below the waist with an upward arc (no spin intent in volley serves), diagonally cross-court beyond the kitchen.
The two-bounce rule: the serve must bounce, the return must bounce — only then may volleys begin.
The kitchen (non-volley zone): you may not volley while touching its line or surface; momentum carrying you in on a volley is a fault.
The ball is in if it touches any line (except a serve touching the kitchen line, which is short).
Odd-numbered scoring positions dictate serving courts (right on even, left on odd) in doubles; singles alternates by score.
Rally scoring is now used in MLP and spreading; USA Pickleball's traditional side-out rules govern most amateur play.
equipment: Paddle
16 in max composite/graphite faces with polymer honeycomb cores; $50-80 beginner, $150-250 pro models — weight (7.3-8.4 oz) matters more than brand.
Balls
Outdoor 40-hole ($3-4 each, they crack), indoor 26-hole softer; buy six — they are the sport's consumable.
Shoes
Court shoes (tennis or dedicated pickleball models) with lateral support and gum soles; replace yearly at heavy play ($90-150).
Court kit
Portable nets ($100-180) and taped lines turn any driveway or tennis court into a pickleball court in minutes.
Grips & eyewear
Overgrips weekly; protective eyewear increasingly standard in sanctioned play.
training: Third-shot reps are the sport's free throws: 100 drops a week (solo into a target, or fed) moves a rating faster than anything else.
Dink endurance: kitchen-line battles train the low, patient posture that decides most doubles points — 15 minutes every session.
Quick-feet intervals: five-court-width shuttles and split-step timing drills; pickleball's first two steps decide most balls.
Wrist and shoulder health: paddles are head-heavy; rotate band work through the week rather than volume-smashing weekends.
Play with better players deliberately — pickleball's community norms (open play, mixed levels) are the best free coaching in sport.
pathway: Open play & club ratings
Community courts and clubs; self- and club-assessed skill ratings (2.0-5.5+) govern most recreational matchmaking.
Amateur tournaments
USA Pickleball-sanctioned brackets by rating and age — thousands of events yearly, a genuine national ladder.
UPTR / DUPR ratings
Dynamic universal ratings (DUPR) unify results across formats; the amateur-pro bridge currency.
Pro tours
PPA Tour and MLP: qualifications, draft-based team rosters, and real prize money since the 2020s boom.
Seniors
The 50+ to 85+ brackets are the sport's deepest and most competitive — pickleball's founding generation still sets records.
events: USA Pickleball National Championships
Since 2009 era at various sites; the amateur sport's showcase week with pro draws.
PPA Tour
The individual professional tour: majors and slams, season-long rankings, the men's and women's stars' home.
Major League Pickleball (MLP)
Team franchises, mixed rosters, dream-breaker finish — the broadcast-era innovation.
US Open Pickleball Championships
Naples, Florida since 2016 — the boomer-era founding festival of the boom.
World & international
The Bainbridge Cup and international federation events grow a genuine world scene beyond North America.
legends: Ben Johns
USA — the sport's dominant #1: triple-crown (singles, doubles, mixed) mastery and the standard of the pro era.
Anna Leigh Waters
USA — teenage #1 across disciplines; the youngest dominant champion in racket sport memory.
Simone Jardim
Brazil/USA — the first great of the organized era: multiple national titles and the women's game's founding star.
Tyson McGuffin
USA — charisma plus championships; the sport's ambassador-carrying title-winner.
The conversion era
Tennis champions from Sam Querrey to Noah Rubin and beyond crossed over in the 2020s — proof the game stands on its own tactics, not just its accessibility.
getting_started: Buy two paddles and six outdoor balls ($120 total); find open play — the culture is famously welcoming to strangers.
Learn the three house rules before playing: two-bounce, kitchen, and only-servers-score (in traditional play).
Practice the third-shot drop against a wall ten minutes daily — it is the whole game's gatekeeper skill.
Play with the strongest group that will have you; pickleball etiquette genuinely levels players up.
Enter a rated amateur tournament within six months — brackets at 3.0 are festivals, not finals.
Watch one pro doubles match: notice how few balls are hit hard, and where every player stands.
glossary: Kitchen
The non-volley zone: seven feet of no-volley real estate on each side of the net.
Dink
A soft volley exchanged from the kitchen line — the game's patience battle.
Third-shot drop
The serving team's soft third ball into the kitchen that unlocks the net.
Two-bounce rule
Serve bounces, return bounces, then volleying begins — the equalizer rule.
Side-out scoring
Traditional doubles scoring where only the serving team can score.
ATP (around the post)
A legal winner struck around — not over — the net post; the sport's circus shot.
Erne
A volley played from beside the kitchen (outside the sideline), legal if airborne around the zone; advanced net piracy.
Nasty Nelson
A serve deliberately bounced into the non-receiving opponent's body zone for a point — gamesmanship, codified.
Dream breaker
MLP's tiebreaking singles rotation, one player per point.
Speed-up
The sudden attack ball from the dink exchange — the gear change that ends or loses the point.

name: Jai Alai
tagline: The fastest ball in sport — 300 km/h out of a woven basket, born in the Basque Country.
overview: Jai alai — Basque pelota played with a long woven cesta strapped to the hand — is played on a three-walled fronton: the ball must be returned off the front wall in one fluid catch-and-throw, and it travels faster than in any other ball sport on record. Guinness lists a 302 km/h throw; the pelota weighs about 190 grams and is livelier than any racket ball, which is why the front is netted and the sport's athletes are genuine sprinting gymnasts with baskets.

'Jai alai' means 'merry festival' in Basque, and the game grew from village fiestas into frontons across the Basque Country, Cuba, Florida, and the Philippines — in Miami, the 1926 fronton made it a betting sport alongside horse racing for seventy years. The Basque professional league (the manista circuit) remains the sport's soul, and pelota is one of the few sports with two national federations in one (Basque and Spanish traditions intertwined).

Newcomers should understand the game is one of pure continuity: no rallies of alternating shapes, but a single unbroken flow — catch the rebote (backwall return), sling, release. Watching a professional partido is watching choreography at highway speed; playing it begins with bare hands (hand-pelota) or a short pala in Basque clubs, which is exactly where every great cesta player started.
facts: Origins
Basque Country mid-19th c. — cestita/pelota vasca; 'jai alai' (merry festival) names the fiesta exhibition games
Governing body
International Federation of Basque Pelota (FIPV, 1929); professional leagues in Spain (LEP / manista circuit) and former Florida frontons
Court (fronton)
36 m long × 10 m wide (juai alai 36 m cancha); front wall of granite, left wall full length; no right wall (open side)
Ball (pelota)
190-200 g core wrapped in latex and goatskin, pressurized; livelier than any racket-sport ball — filled by hand, replaced mid-game
Cesta
Wicker basket 60-70 cm, curved, strapped to the throwing hand; catching and releasing are one motion
Record speed
302 km/h (José Ramón Areitio, Rhode Island 1979) — the fastest measured ball speed in any sport
Scoring
Partido scoring to a fixed target (traditionally 30-40 points) or match-play 'quiniela' rounds to 7 in fronton formats
history: Basque villages play bare-hand pelota against church walls; leather and basket implements evolve from injured hands.
The cesta appears; the first trinquete and fronton courts are built in the Basque Country and Cuba (Havana frontons).
Miami Jai-Alai fronton opens — Florida parimutuel betting fuses the sport with gambling for seven decades.
Golden era: Cuban, Filipino, and Basque professionals; Connecticut and Rhode Island frontons pack thousands nightly.
Cuba and Florida decline (politics, casinos, strikes); the Basque professional league carries the sport's elite level.
2000s-today

Miami's fronton closes (2021 the sport ends there); Ocala and Dania carry US jai alai on; Basque pelota thrives professionally with televised manista seasons, and FIPV amateur worlds spread the family of codes (hand, pala, cesta, remonte).
formats: Partido
The classic singles or doubles match to a fixed point total (30-40); the Basque professional format.
Quiniela (fronton jai alai)
Rotation format of 8 players-pairs, first to 7 points, positions cycling after each point — designed for pari-mutuel betting.
Remonte
The most virtuosic code: a shorter, shallower cesta with no catching — the ball must be kept in continuous play, lifted on the fly.
The pelota family
Hand-pelota (bare hands), pala (flat wooden bat), share frontons and the Basque club calendar — jai alai is one branch of the tree.
skills: Catch-and-throw (cesta)
The whole sport in one motion: receive the ball into the basket's pocket and slingshot it out in a single arc — stopping the ball kills the rally.
Wall work: 100 catch-throw cycles per session against the front wall at increasing pace, both sides of the body.
Rebote (backwall play)
Letting the ball fly to the back wall to catch its return high and behind — the sport's timing masterclass.
Coach hits deep balls: player must catch each behind the 11 m line on the rebote, 40 reps weekly.
Left-side & right-side play
Singles specialists own one wall: the rebote-catch forehand side demands different geometry from the front-side game.
Position drills: alternate front-wall returns and rebote catches in sequence, 15 minutes continuous.
Servicio (serve)
The serve must land in a marked zone (between lines 4 and 7); it begins every point with placement intent.
40 serves per session to the corners of the legal zone; count first-point win rates.
Chiquita & carom play
The low dying ball along the wall and deliberate side-wall angles that break an opponent's rhythm.
Target zones chalked on the left wall: 30 chiquitas low along the wall, 30 angled caroms per week.
Match conditioning
Jai alai is sprint gymnastics: repeated maximal throws with sprint recoveries demand brutal short-burst fitness.
Intervals: 20 s sprint / 40 s walk × 10, twice weekly, plus rotational med-ball throws 3×10 each side.
rules: The ball must strike the front wall above a low line and within the side boundaries; it may first touch the left (long) wall.
A return is good if it lands beyond the foul (short) lines — marked numbered lines define the serve zone and the valid landing area.
The receiver must catch and return in one motion — juggling, holding, or a double touch loses the point.
Interference and obstruction rules protect players sharing the court's left-wall space; safety lines govern serve reception.
Quiniela scoring: rotation of 8 post positions, point to the rally winner, first to 7 wins; ties settle by weiter play in betting formats.
The pelota is replaced by the judge when it loses liveliness — each one is handmade and match-grade for a few games only.
Spectators sit behind netting; the 200 km/h pelota makes protective screens structural, not decorative.
equipment: Cesta
Hand-woven Spanish chestnut reed, 60-70 cm, custom-bent to the player's hand; $200-600, lasting weeks at pro intensity.
Pelota
Hand-wrapped goatskin over a rubber-latex core, ~190 g; match balls $80-120 each — the sport's costly heart.
Fronton
Granite front wall (the cancha's bounce defines the game), left wall, numbered floor lines; 36 m courts for cesta codes.
Kit
White fronton tradition: sash colors mark teams or post positions; helmets not worn at pro level — placement and etiquette are the safety system.
Bare-hand & pala gear
The sibling codes' needs: taped hands and leather gloves for hand-pelota; solid wooden palas for the flat-bat codes.
training: Fronton repetition is everything: 400-600 catch-throw contacts weekly at graduated pace builds the single-motion throw.
Sprint intervals and lateral shuttles match the sport's effort profile — maximal bursts with incomplete recovery.
Rotational power: med-ball slings mimicking the cesta arc, 3×10 each side, plus shoulder and elbow prehab daily (the sling's torque is enormous).
Play the family codes: hand-pelota builds touch and courage; remonte builds continuous-play reflexes that transfuse into jai alai.
Study partido tape: positioning on the rebote and serve patterns decide elite matches more than raw throw speed.
pathway: Basque club pelota
Every village fronton: children begin with bare hands and pala before the cesta — the traditional ladder.
Youth federated play
Regional and Spanish junior pelota championships across the code family.
Professional manista circuit
Basque professional contracts (the remonte and cesta leagues) — small, elite, culturally central.
International frontons
Historic circuits in Florida (Dania, Ocala), the Philippines, Mexico, and Italy employed professionals across eras.
Amateur & FIPV worlds
World Pelota Championships (every 4 years, since 1952 for the amateur codes) unite the diaspora.
events: Manista professional seasons
The Basque professional league's winter and summer tournaments — the sport's elite calendar.
Campeonato Manos Parejas & Cuatro y Medio
Basque championship classics across the codes (hand-pelota's famous finals fill 10,000-seat frontons).
Florida fronton seasons
Dania Jai-Alai and Ocala's seasons: quiniela racing for parimutuel nights — the American remnant of the golden era.
FIPV World Pelota Championships
Amateur worlds across all codes and nations — the Basque diaspora's Olympic moment.
Exhibition festivals
Jai alai's fiesta roots persist: exhibition partidos at Basque festivals worldwide, from Boise to Buenos Aires.
legends: José Ramón Areitio
Spain — threw the 302 km/h Guinness-record ball (1979); the sport's measured summit.
Joey Cornblit
Cuba/USA — Miami's superstar of the 1970s-80s, a fronton-era celebrity who carried American jai alai.
Retegui family
Basque pelota royalty: Retegi I and II dominated hand-pelota championships across two generations.
The Retegui dynasty
Basque pelota royalty: Retegi I and Retegi II dominated hand-pelota championships across two generations — the fronton's royal family.
The remonte masters
The one-touch code's specialists — players who never catch the ball at all, keeping it alive in continuous flight.
getting_started: Watch first: a partido video (Euskal Telebista streams the manista season) teaches the flow in ten minutes.
Start with the family: bare-hand or pala pelota at a Basque club or school if accessible — the cesta comes later for most players.
Visit a living fronton — Dania (Florida) or any Basque court — and feel the pelota's report off granite before judging the sport.
If learning cesta, budget for coaching: the single-motion catch-throw is unlearnable solo from scratch.
Respect the safety geometry from day one: the ball's speed makes positioning discipline the first lesson, not the last.
Read the quiniela program at a fronton night: betting-free, the rotation format is still a fascinating tactical machine.
glossary: Cesta
The woven basket-glove; the sport's defining tool.
Pelota
The hand-wrapped ball — livelier and faster than any other in sport.
Fronton
The three-walled court; 'cancha' its playing floor.
Rebote
The back-wall return and the art of catching it high behind.
Quiniela
The 8-player rotation format built for parimutuel betting.
Partido
The classic match to a fixed point total.
Remonte
The no-catch code: continuous play with a shallow cesta.
Chiquita
The low, dying ball glued along the wall.
Manista
A professional pelota player (from mano, hand — the family's root code).
Jai alai
'Merry festival' in Basque — the game's name is its birth certificate.
